ideas.name: RigRiot
ideas.niche: VTuber avatar quality assurance and technical pre-flight diagnostics.
ideas.problem: High-energy streamers suffer from 'mesh breaking' and 'physics explosions'—visual glitches where the avatar's face deforms unnaturally or accessories fly away during intense emotional outbursts or rapid head movements.
ideas.targetUser: Indie VTubers and technical artists at VTuber agencies who need to validate 3D (VRM) or 2D (Live2D) models for stability before live broadcasts.
coreFeatures: Chaos Macro Engine (simulates rapid, erratic head and neck movement patterns)
Expression Stress Matrix (cycles through all facial blendshapes at 150% intensity)
Vertex Deformation Heatmap (visual overlays highlighting areas of extreme mesh stretching)
Physics Clipping Log (records instances of hair, clothing, or accessory collision failures)
realDependencies: Unity or Unreal Engine runtime for real-time 3D rendering
Live2D Cubism SDK or VRM file parsers
Compute Shaders for real-time vertex delta calculation
GPU-accelerated physics engine (PhysX or Havok)
ideas.emulationStrategy: The demo will utilize a generic 3D humanoid model with a procedural 'stress texture.' Instead of real vertex analysis, it will overlay a noise-based red heatmap that increases in density based on a simulated 'stress variable.' Movement will be faked using a high-frequency sine-wave animation loop. The 'Collision Log' will be a mock console window that triggers randomized string-based error messages (e.g., 'Collision Detected: Accessory_Hair_L') timed to the peaks of the movement animation. Model loading will be simulated with a scripted 3-second delay and a progress bar.

ideas.name: AuralOrbit
ideas.niche: Visual 3D spatial planning for binaural ASMR content creators
ideas.problem: The difficulty of visualizing and sequencing complex ear-to-ear audio movements, leading to repetitive and unengaging listener experiences.
ideas.targetUser: Independent ASMR creators and specialized sound designers who produce spatialized content for platforms like YouTube and Patreon.
coreFeatures: 3D Spatial Canvas with icon-based trigger placement
Timeline-based movement sequencer
Intensity and Proximity curve editor
Pre-set movement pattern templates
realDependencies: Three.js for 3D spatial rendering
Web Audio API for binaural audio playback simulation
AWS S3 for project and audio asset storage
Firebase for user authentication and cloud syncing
ideas.emulationStrategy: Replace Three.js with a 2D HTML5 Canvas simulating a top-down view of a head. Use local .mp3 assets for triggers and manipulate volume/panning via standard HTML5 Audio to mimic spatiality. Substitute AWS/Firebase with localStorage for project persistence. Implement 'Network Simulation' by wrapping all save/load functions in async calls with randomized 500ms-2000ms delays and 'Loading...' UI states.

ideas.name: LayerFail
ideas.problem: Educational content creators lack a structured, searchable visual database for 3D printing failure modes, leading to inefficient asset management and inconsistent technical documentation when producing tutorials.
ideas.targetUser: Technical 3D printing YouTubers, TikTok/Reels educators, and MakerSpace instructors who require a standardized way to catalog and retrieve visual evidence of print errors for instructional use.
coreFeatures: High-Resolution Failure Capture & Metadata Mapping
Standardized Failure Taxonomy (e.g., Warping, Stringing, Underextrusion)
Slicer Configuration Auto-Extraction via OCR
Curated 'Video Asset' Collections for rapid scene sourcing
realDependencies: AWS S3 (Cloud media storage for high-res failure photos/videos)
PostgreSQL (Relational database for complex tagging and taxonomy)
Google Cloud Vision API (OCR to extract print settings from slicer screenshots)
Auth0 (Secure user authentication and creator profiles)
ideas.emulationStrategy: The demo will utilize a local JSON manifest containing 20 pre-defined failure entries to simulate a populated database. Media uploads will be emulated using a `setTimeout` function that triggers a simulated 2-second progress bar before returning a local Blob URL. The OCR feature will be faked with a 'Scanning...' UI overlay that, after a 1.5-second delay, populates text fields using a hardcoded dictionary mapped to specific mock filenames. Authentication will be simulated via a single boolean flag in LocalStorage.

ideas.name: StitchStress
ideas.niche: Digital garment deformation and texture integrity previewing for metaverse-ready assets.
ideas.problem: The high-friction, time-consuming cycle of exporting 3D assets to heavy simulation software or game engines just to verify texture warping and mesh clipping during movement.
ideas.targetUser: Digital fashion designers and 3D asset creators (specifically those working with CLO3D, Marvelous Designer, or Blender) who produce wearables for platforms like Roblox, Decentraland, or Unreal Engine.
coreFeatures: Mocap-Driven Stress Loops (preset animation suites for walking, dancing, and crouching)
Dynamic Texture Heatmaps (visualizing pixel dilation and stretch thresholds)
Automated Mesh Clipping Detection (flagging geometry intersections with the avatar)
Engine-Specific Constraint Validation (checking texture density for mobile vs. desktop engines)
realDependencies: Three.js or Babylon.js for high-fidelity WebGL rendering
GLTF/FBX file parsing libraries for asset ingestion
Physics-based cloth simulation engine (e.g., Ammo.js or PhysX) for real-time deformation
Mixamo or similar MoCap API for animation data integration
ideas.emulationStrategy: The demo will bypass real mesh-collision physics by using a vertex shader to simulate color-coded 'heat' (red/blue) based on the animation timestamp and a predefined 'stress map'. File uploads will be replaced by a static 'Load Sample Asset' button that triggers a 3-second simulated loading state with a progress bar. The 'Stress Analysis Report' will be a mock JSON object returned after a fake 'Analyzing Geometry' delay, providing deterministic but artificial coordinates for 'texture stretching' and 'clipping' triggered by specific animation keyframes.

ideas.name: LuminaSync
ideas.problem: The 'floating subject' effect where physical lighting (direction, color, and intensity) fails to match the digital environment, breaking the illusion of realism in green-screen or AI-backgrounded video.
ideas.targetUser: Mid-tier Twitch/YouTube streamers, professional remote presenters, and digital content creators who use virtual backgrounds but lack professional studio lighting expertise.
coreFeatures: Background Light Profiler: Automatically analyzes a selected virtual background to extract the primary light source vector, Kelvin temperature, and light intensity.
AR Shadow Map Overlay: Projects a real-time augmented reality light-map over the user's webcam feed to show exactly where shadows should fall on their face and body.
Live Lighting Calibration: A step-by-step corrective UI that gives specific commands like 'Shift key light 15 degrees left' or 'Increase warmth by 200K' to match the scene.
Depth-Blur Validator: Compares the subject's edge sharpness and focal plane with the background's depth map to ensure consistent bokeh and spatial depth.
realDependencies: MediaPipe or OpenCV for facial landmarks and depth estimation
Webcam/MediaDevices API for real-time video stream access
Computer Vision models for light source direction estimation (Light Estimation API)
High-fidelity colorimeter-style software processing for Kelvin matching
ideas.emulationStrategy: The demo will bypass heavy CV computation by using a 'Scenario Library' of pre-defined environment profiles (e.g., 'Golden Hour Cafe', 'Neon Cyberpunk', 'Dim Office'). When a user 'uploads' a background, the app will fetch hardcoded JSON metadata (direction: [x,y,z], color: #hex, intensity: 0.8) corresponding to that profile. The 'Real-time Overlay' will be a static SVG layer drawn over the webcam feed based on these preset coordinates. To simulate heavy processing, all 'Analysis' actions will use a 2000ms setTimeout to trigger a loading state. The 'Match Score' will be a pseudo-random value that increments slightly every time the user clicks a 'Simulated Adjustment' button, giving the illusion of a real-time calibration loop.
